description: Test your knowledge of PA SK1 | Skin: normal architecture, UV damage, and actinic keratosis pathology.

cards.text: What are the two main cellular layers of skin and which is avascular?
cards.answer: The epidermis (stratified squamous epithelium; avascular) and dermis (collagen-rich connective tissue; vascular). Keratinocytes comprise 90% of epidermal cells.

cards.text: Contrast UVB and UVA in terms of wavelength and mechanism of skin cancer.
cards.answer: UVB (280–315 nm) directly damages DNA causing TP53 mutations—dominant carcinogen in SCC/BCC. UVA (315–400 nm) penetrates deeper, generates ROS, damages melanocytes—linked to melanoma.

tip.tip: UVB = direct DNA damage (TP53); UVA = deep penetration & oxidative stress

cards.text: What defines malignancy in skin epithelial tumours?
cards.answer: Invasion through the dermo-epidermal junction (DEJ)—breach of the basement membrane. This distinguishes in-situ (confined to epidermis) from invasive disease.

tip.tip: DEJ breach = invasion = malignancy; intact DEJ = in-situ (non-invasive)

cards.text: List three cardinal clinical features of actinic keratosis.
cards.answer: Rough, scaly, erythematous plaques on sun-exposed skin (face, scalp, dorsal hands); sandpaper texture on palpation; usually <1 cm; multiple lesions common.

tip.tip: SAND = Scaly AND erythematous; sun-exposed; multiple (field effect)

cards.text: What is the key histological hallmark distinguishing AK from invasive SCC?
cards.answer: Atypical keratinocytes confined to basal and spinous layers with NO breach of basement membrane. Solar elastosis (blue-grey degenerated elastic fibres) is diagnostic evidence of UV damage.

tip.tip: AK = atypical + intact basement = in-situ; SCC = atypical + breached basement = invasive

cards.text: What is 'field cancerisation' and why is it clinically important in AK treatment?
cards.answer: Entire sun-exposed skin surface accumulates cumulative UV mutations over decades. One visible AK means surrounding skin carries the same damage; topical field treatment is required to prevent progression in adjacent areas.

tip.tip: One AK = field of damage; treat the field, not just the lesion

cards.text: What is the annual progression rate of actinic keratosis to invasive SCC?
cards.answer: Approximately 0.1–1% of individual AKs per year progress to invasive SCC. However, patients with multiple AKs carry cumulative lifetime risk; ~25% regress untreated.

tip.tip: Low annual risk per lesion, but high cumulative risk with multiple lesions = why treat early

cards.text: Which patient populations develop actinic keratosis earliest and most aggressively?
cards.answer: Fitzpatrick skin types I–II (fair, burns easily); outdoor workers/farmers; age >50; immunosuppressed patients (e.g. transplant recipients develop AKs in 30s–40s).

tip.tip: Fair skin + sun + immunosuppression = early/aggressive AK risk
